chunks: "The main idea is that I route the two traces as a single object. Same layer, parallel the whole way, constant spacing, same length, same number of vias, same neighbours.
Anything that makes one trace see a different environment than the other turns differential signal into common-mode.

In detail: I set the width and spacing from the stackup so the differential impedance hits its target, 100 ohms for most standards or 90 for USB, and I keep that spacing constant along the whole run, only opening it up briefly at the pins.
I route over a solid reference plane and avoid anything under the pair that could differ between the two traces, like a plane edge or a via field.
Bends are symmetric 45 degrees or arcs, and the outer trace of a bend is longer, so I add a little jog on the inner trace right after the bend instead of waiting till the end.
At layer changes I use two identical vias, with ground vias next to them for the return current.
AC coupling caps get placed symmetric, side by side, at the same place along both traces.

What's different from single-ended is that the matching is within the pair, in picoseconds, and that I care about keeping the pair together; the clearance to other signals should be several times the gap between the two traces, and I don't want stubs, test points, or one side detouring around an obstacle."
